title: September/October 2026
gist: The table of contents for Foreign Affairs' September/October 2026 issue (Volume 105, No. 5) reveals the magazine's editorial focus: the fracturing of the U.S.-led alliance and Middle East order after the Iran war, China's economic and rare-earth leverage, and AI's dual-use security risks.

themes.theme: Editorial focus signals elite discourse priorities

insights.claim: Foreign Affairs' September/October 2026 issue leads with two directly competing frameworks for the post-American order: Kurt Campbell and Rush Doshi's case that U.S. alliances will survive and strengthen, versus Mark Leonard's case that the U.S.-led order has already been abandoned — reflecting genuine, unresolved disagreement among senior former U.S. and European officials about alliance durability.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: The existence of this live debate among top-tier foreign-policy insiders itself is a signal that alliance-durability uncertainty (and its knock-on effects for defense spending, trade blocs, and currency arrangements) is a genuinely open question rather than a settled consensus.
insights.quote: How Alliances Survive The Case Against Pessimism and the Path to a New Allied Order Kurt M. Campbell and Rush Doshi The Abandoned Order Learning to Live in a Post-American World Mark Leonard

insights.claim: The issue treats the collapse of the American-led Middle East order (via Marc Lynch's and F. Gregory Gause III's essays) and the unraveling of the global alliance order (via Campbell/Doshi and Leonard) as the two dominant geopolitical narratives of the moment, both tied directly to the fallout from the 2026 U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: Signals that the Iran war's regional and alliance-system aftershocks are viewed by elite commentators as the defining geopolitical event of 2026, worth tracking for follow-on effects on Gulf energy security and U.S. basing.
insights.quote: The End of the American Middle East Iran and the Last Gasp of a Failed Order Marc Lynch The New Old Middle East Wars of Sound and Fury F. Gregory Gause III

insights.claim: The issue frames China's overcapacity as the trigger for 'the next global economic crisis' and separately profiles China's rare-earth dominance as its 'most potent weapon,' indicating that Chinese industrial and resource leverage is treated as the top China-related economic security concern of the period.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: Two separate lead essays converging on Chinese overcapacity and rare-earth leverage as distinct risk vectors suggests investors should watch both channels — trade/dumping risk and critical-minerals supply-chain risk — as live, elevated concerns among policy elites.
insights.quote: The Next Global Economic Crisis Could Be Made in China How Overcapacity Ends Michael B. G. Froman How China Found Its Most Potent Weapon The Real History of Beijing’s Rare-Earth Dominance Gloria Xiong and Jessica Chen Weiss

insights.claim: AI's dual-use security risk is elevated to first-tier national-security status alongside alliance and Middle East order breakdown, with a lead essay devoted specifically to AI-enabled bioweapons risk.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: Positions AI-bio convergence risk as a mainstream national-security concern rather than a fringe topic, relevant for biosecurity and AI-safety policy and investment tracking.
insights.quote: AI and the New Age of Bioweapons Preparing for a World of Synthetic Pathogens Elizabeth Sherwood-Randall
